summary: Records a format for operators to publish their own mapping from IP address prefixes to simple, coarse-grained location information. Interested parties can poll the feeds and combine them with other geolocation data.

eli5.summary: A company posts a list saying roughly which city each of its addresses is in, so others do not have to guess.

subtitle: A plain CSV file where a network operator tells everyone roughly where its IP address ranges are located.

tldr.problem: Services guess where an IP address is, and when an operator moves a prefix, there is no central way to tell everyone, so the guess goes stale and users see degraded service.
tldr.mechanism: The operator publishes a text file with one CSV line per IP prefix: prefix, country code, region, city and (deprecated) postal code. Consumers poll the file and merge it with their other geolocation data.
tldr.outcome: The format only carries coarse location, is informational, and is described as already deployed. Section 7 says a new, more extensible format is planned.

today: RFC 8805 is an Informational document from the Independent Submission stream, and it has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. Its own text says a new format is planned, since this one is hard to extend.

sections.title: Why Operators Publish Their Own Location Data
sections.content:
Internet services use best-effort IP geolocation to send traffic to the nearest serving location, to infer a likely native language, and to add context to search queries. When an ISP moves a prefix to a new place, those services can start to perform badly, and customers may complain to the ISP.

The trouble is that there is no centralized way to tell every interested consumer about a change. RFC 8805 records a format, colloquially called a geolocation feed, in which a network operator publishes a mapping from IP prefixes to simplified location. Interested parties poll and parse the feeds and merge them with other data sources.

The text says this is a currently deployed format. It names Google as one consumer and says a significant number of ISPs use it. The operators that first used it were regional operators and technical conferences whose networks move from one conference location to the next.
sections.eli5: If a shop moves to a new street, it is easier if the shop tells the map makers than if they have to find out by themselves. This is a way for network owners to tell the map makers.

sections.title: The Feed File Format
sections.content:
A feed is a text file in UTF-8. Lines end in CRLF, blank lines are ignored, and anything from a hash character to the end of the line is a comment. The RFC points out that comments are not part of the CSV specification in RFC 4180.

Every other line is a CSV entry of the form ip_prefix,alpha2code,region,city,postal_code. Only the IP prefix is REQUIRED; the other fields are OPTIONAL and may be empty, though the required number of commas SHOULD still be present.

For simplicity, a feed should describe all the addresses the publisher wants to publish, not only the ones that changed. The RFC says that publishing only changes is likely to be too complex to operate.
sections.eli5: Each line of the file is one row of a spreadsheet: which addresses, which country, which region and which city. Only the addresses are a must.

sections.title: The Entry Fields
sections.content:
• IP prefix: a single IP address or a prefix in CIDR notation, IPv4 or IPv6, such as 192.0.2.0/24 or 2001:db8::/32.
  • alpha2code: a 2-letter ISO 3166-1 alpha 2 country code such as US, JP or PL. Parsers SHOULD treat it case-insensitively. Older versions called this field country.
  • region: an ISO 3166-2 region code, such as ID-RI.
  • city: free UTF-8 text without a comma, such as Dublin.
  • postal code: marked OPTIONAL, DEPRECATED. Parsers should still accept it, but new feeds SHOULD NOT include it because it is too precise.

To say that a prefix has no location information, leave all four location fields blank, for example 192.0.2.0/24,,,,. The code ZZ has historically been used for this, but is not necessarily preferred.
sections.eli5: You can say as much or as little as you like: just a country, or a country and a city. The street-level code is discouraged because it points too closely at people.

sections.title: Parsing and Consuming a Feed
sections.content:
Entries with a missing or unparseable IP prefix MUST be discarded. Duplicate entries are an error, and consumers SHOULD log them. Nested prefixes are allowed, and consumers SHOULD use the longest matching prefix as the best match for an address. Entries whose optional fields fail to parse SHOULD be discarded, and logging them is RECOMMENDED. A parser MUST ignore extra fields beyond those it expects.

Consumers MAY treat a feed as a hint only and prefer other sources. They SHOULD protect integrity by fetching the feed in a way that guarantees it, for example HTTP over TLS. They SHOULD also verify that the publisher is authoritative for the prefixes it lists, and ignore and log entries that fail the check. Accuracy checks and handling of discrepancies are left to the consumer.

Because a publisher can change the data at any time, consumers SHOULD refresh periodically: with no other information, no less often than weekly. A publisher MAY signal refresh timing with the standard HTTP Expires or Cache-Control max-age headers.
sections.eli5: A reader should check that the sender really owns the addresses they are describing, and should look at the file again every so often because it can change.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Publishers are advised to consider the privacy implications for the users of the described networks before publishing. Each location field is optional so that a publisher can share only the level of detail it finds acceptable. The postal code can pinpoint a location, sometimes within a building, so such values MUST NOT be published without the express consent of the people being located.

On security, the RFC argues that self-publishing opens no new attack vectors, since there is no true security in hiding where an address is. It does note that a feed can make it easier to tell prefixes full of customers from unused ones. Consumers may fetch feeds from hostile sources, so they must validate input. A consumer that does not verify authority could let one ISP make claims about address space held by another. At the time of writing only out-of-band checks are implemented, such as comparing a feed with public allocation data.
sections.eli5: A feed should only say how much about a place the owner is happy to share. Readers should be careful, because anybody could try to send them a fake list.

sections.title: Limits, Discovery and Future Work
sections.content:
The RFC does not formally say how to find or verify feeds. In practice, feeds have been shared as HTTPS URIs exchanged by email, and checked by personal knowledge of the parties or by comparing the listed prefixes with the BGP-advertised prefixes of known autonomous systems. The text says this is unlikely to be adequate for long-term, widespread use. Earlier ideas based on WHOIS or DNS were removed because, to the authors' knowledge, they were never implemented.

Because the format is hard to extend, no extensions are anticipated. The authors say they plan to write a document for a new format, possibly based on JSON, and that extensibility will be part of that new design. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Right now people swap links by email, which works for small groups but not for the whole world. The authors expect a better list format to come later.
